newsitem.title: USA: Saudi envoy hopes U.S. concerns allayed on bombing.
newsitem.headline: Saudi envoy hopes U.S. concerns allayed on bombing.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's defence minister said after meeting President Bill Clinton on Tuesday that he hoped he allayed U.S. concerns about the investigation into last year's bombing against Americans in the kingdom.
"I think if you ask the American side you will find a positive response that they were left with," Saudi Defence Minister Prince Sultan, who is also a deputy prime minister, told reporters.
U.S. officials were circumspect, saying the issue was brought up and would continue to be a subject of discussion.

The visit by the prince, heading a high-level ministerial delegation, was meant to reaffirm close U.S.-Saudi relations marred by U.S. concerns over the probe into last June's truck bombing that killed 19 American servicemen near Dhahran.
Washington has complained publicly that Saudi Arabia is not sharing enough information on its investigation.

A White House statement said that during the talks, Clinton "stressed his determination to protect the security of American troops stationed in Saudi Arabia, and they discussed our cooperation in the fight against terrorism."

A White House official, speaking on condition of anonymity, declined to elaborate. "All I can tell you from our perspective is the issue was raised and is something we continue to discuss with them," the official said.

In a reminder of the continued threat in Saudi Arabia, the U.S. embassy there warned Americans in the kingdom on Tuesday to raise their guard against further attacks following fresh threats by a leading Islamic dissident.
Clinton reaffirmed the U.S. commitment to ensuring security and stability in the Gulf region and pledged to "work with Saudi Arabia to respond to any external threats to our mutual interests."

Prince Sultan said he and Clinton did not discuss Saudi Arabia's interest in purchasing perhaps as many as 100 F-16 fighters to replace their ageing fleet of 114 F-5s. Israel has expressed concern about a possible deal.
"This visit was not here to conclude armament deals or contracts," the prince said. He spoke in Arabic translated into English by Prince Bandar, the Saudi ambassador to America.
Generally speaking, both sides spoke glowingly of the state of U.S.-Saudi relations.

"I would like to reaffirm the especially strong relationship between the United States and Saudi Arabia," said Prince Sultan, who said he passed along congratulations from King Fahd on Clinton's re-election to a second term.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said: "U.S.-Saudi relations are strong and will remain so. Our countries have been friends in peace and allies in war."

Prince Sultan, representing his brother King Fahd, arrived on Monday evening at the head of a delegation that includes foreign, oil and trade ministers and a deputy finance minister. They will stay until Friday.

Prince Sultan was to meet Defence Secretary William Cohen on Wednesday and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Thursday to discuss, among other topics, the Middle East peace process. The prince described Clinton's Middle East policy as "steady and consistent."
